goals: State why a democracy needs an independent judiciary and what independence means
Explain how independence is secured: appointment, tenure, finance and other protections
Present the debate on appointment of judges in a balanced way
Describe the structure of the integrated judiciary, Article 141 and Article 129

slides.heading: Judiciary: Independence and Structure
slides.body_md: Part 1: why we need an **independent judiciary**, how its **independence** is secured, and how the **courts** are arranged.

nodes.label: Why an independent judiciary
What independence means
How it is secured
The appointment debate
Structure of the courts

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why an independent judiciary, what independence means, how it is secured, the appointment debate, and the structure of the courts
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: When two people disagree, or when a government and a citizen disagree, someone must decide fairly. That is the work of the judiciary. In this part we ask why the judiciary must be independent, how the Constitution secures that independence, and how the courts of India are organised.

slides.heading: Why we need an independent judiciary

rows: Applies the same law to everyone, including the government
Decides disputes between citizens, between citizens and the government, and between governments
Enforces Fundamental Rights and other rights against wrongful acts
Examines laws and actions against the Constitution

visual.alt: Table of four roles of the judiciary: upholding the rule of law, settling disputes, protecting rights and guarding the Constitution

slides.narration: A democracy needs the judiciary for four reasons. It upholds the rule of law, so that the law applies to everyone, including the government. It settles disputes. It protects rights. And it guards the Constitution by examining laws and actions that may go against it. To do these tasks fairly, it must be independent.

slides.heading: What independence means

rows: Freedom from interference by the legislature and the executive
That judges answer to no one
Deciding cases on law and evidence
That judges may ignore the Constitution
That the judiciary runs the country

visual.alt: Table contrasting what independence of the judiciary means with what it does not mean
visual.caption: Accountability remains: reasoned judgments in open court, the Constitution, and removal for proved misbehaviour.

slides.narration: Independence means freedom from interference by the legislature and the executive when judges decide cases. It does not mean that judges answer to no one. They are bound by the Constitution, they give reasons for their decisions in open court, and they can be removed for proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

visual.caption: How independence of the judiciary is secured.

slides.narration: This web shows the safeguards around the judiciary. There is a method of appointment, security of tenure, financial independence, protection from debate in the legislature and the power of courts to punish for contempt. Each safeguard closes one way in which pressure could be put on a judge. We study them one by one.

slides.heading: Appointment of judges

rows: The Supreme Court's view: the Chief Justice of India and a collegium of senior judges play the decisive role in recommending names
The National Judicial Appointments Commission Act passed
The Act was struck down by the Supreme Court

visual.alt: Table on appointment of judges: the President appoints; since the Second Judges case of 1993 the Chief Justice of India and a collegium play the decisive role in recommending names; the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act was passed in 2014 and struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015
visual.caption: Position as of 2024.

slides.narration: Judges are appointed by the President. Since the Second Judges case in nineteen ninety three, the Supreme Court has taken the view that the Chief Justice of India and a collegium of senior judges play the decisive role in recommending names. In twenty fourteen Parliament passed an Act to set up a commission. The Supreme Court struck it down in twenty fifteen.

slides.heading: From recommendation to appointment

nodes.label: The Chief Justice of India and a collegium of senior judges recommend names
The names go to the government
The President appoints the judges

visual.alt: Flow of appointment to the Supreme Court: the Chief Justice of India and a collegium recommend names, the names go to the government, and the President appoints the judges
visual.caption: Appointment to the Supreme Court

slides.narration: In practice, for the Supreme Court, the Chief Justice of India and a collegium of senior judges recommend names. The names go to the government. The President then appoints the judges. The formal power is the President's, but the recommendation carries great weight. This is the position as of twenty twenty four.

slides.body_md: In which year did the Supreme Court strike down the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act?
slides.narration: Recall the year of the decision.

slides.heading: The appointment debate

rows: The collegium keeps appointments free from pressure by the executive
A wider body that is accountable to the public should also take part
Senior judges are best placed to judge who is fit to serve
The process should be more open and transparent
A commission with outside members could weaken independence
A commission could share the responsibility among the organs

visual.alt: Table of the debate on the appointment of judges: some argue the collegium protects independence, that senior judges know best, and that a commission could weaken independence; others argue for a wider accountable body, for more openness, and that a commission could share responsibility

slides.narration: People debate how judges should be chosen. Some argue that the collegium keeps appointments free from pressure by the executive, and that senior judges know best who is fit to serve. Others argue that a wider body that is accountable to the public should also take part, and that the process should be more open. Students should weigh the reasons.

slides.heading: Security of tenure

rows: Supreme Court judges at 65; High Court judges at 62
A special majority in both Houses
Removal is very difficult, so judges are free from pressure

visual.alt: Table on security of tenure: Supreme Court judges retire at 65 and High Court judges at 62; only Parliament can remove a judge, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by a special majority in both Houses; this makes removal very difficult and protects judges from pressure
visual.caption: Special majority: a majority of the total membership of each House and at least two thirds of the members present and voting.

slides.narration: Supreme Court judges retire at sixty five and High Court judges at sixty two. A judge can be removed only by Parliament, on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by a special majority in both Houses. This means a majority of the total membership of each House and at least two thirds of those present and voting. It is a very difficult process.

slides.heading: How a judge can be removed

nodes.label: A motion to remove is moved in a House of Parliament
A committee inquires into the charge
Each House passes it by a special majority
The President orders the removal

visual.alt: Flow of removal of a judge: a motion is moved in a House of Parliament, a committee inquires into the charge, each House passes it by a special majority, and the President orders the removal
visual.caption: Removal of a judge

slides.narration: A motion for removal is moved in a House of Parliament. A committee inquires into the charge. Each House must then pass the motion by a special majority. Finally the President orders the removal. Because every step is demanding, a judge does not have to fear losing office for an unwelcome ruling.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a Chief Minister's announcement
slides.body_md: The Chief Minister of imagined Varunadesh announces the dismissal of a High Court judge. Test the claim.
bullets: On which ground, and by what majority?

headers: Applying the safeguards to imagined Varunadesh
rows: Who can remove a High Court judge?
Parliament only, not a Chief Minister
Proved misbehaviour or incapacity, not unwelcome rulings
A special majority in both Houses
Result of the Chief Minister's announcement

visual.alt: Worked example table: the Chief Minister of imagined Varunadesh announces the dismissal of a High Court judge; only Parliament can remove a judge, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by a special majority in both Houses, so the announcement has no legal effect
visual.caption: Judges are safe from pressure over their rulings.

slides.narration: Let us test the claim. Who can remove a High Court judge? Only Parliament, and not a Chief Minister. On what ground? Proved misbehaviour or incapacity, not unwelcome rulings. By what majority? A special majority in both Houses. So the announcement has no legal effect, and the judge continues in office.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false
slides.body_md: Independence of the judiciary means that judges are free from every kind of accountability.
slides.narration: Think about what independence does and does not mean.

slides.heading: Finance, debate and contempt

rows: Salaries and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and are not voted on
The conduct of judges cannot be discussed in the legislature, except during removal proceedings

visual.alt: Table of the other safeguards: salaries and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund and are not voted on; the conduct of judges is not discussed in the legislature except during removal; courts can punish for contempt

slides.narration: Three more safeguards. The salaries and allowances of judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, so they are not voted on. The conduct of judges cannot be discussed in the legislature except during removal proceedings. And the courts can punish for contempt, which protects their authority and dignity.

visual.caption: The court hierarchy of India.

slides.narration: The courts form a pyramid. The Supreme Court is at the top, with the Chief Justice of India and thirty three other judges, thirty four in all, as of twenty twenty four. High Courts are in the states. District and subordinate courts are below them. Appeals go upward through this single hierarchy.

slides.heading: An integrated judiciary

rows: One hierarchy of courts, not separate Union and state systems
The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts
The Supreme Court is a court of record: its decisions are preserved as records, and it can punish for its own contempt
The Chief Justice of India and 33 other judges, 34 in all, as of 2024; Parliament can change the number by law

visual.alt: Table of features of the integrated judiciary: one hierarchy; Article 141, Supreme Court law binds all courts; Article 129, court of record; strength of 34 judges in all as of 2024

slides.narration: India has an integrated judiciary: one hierarchy of courts, and not separate systems for the Union and the states. Article one hundred and forty one makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts. Under Article one hundred and twenty nine the Supreme Court is a court of record, which means its decisions are preserved as records, and it can punish for its own contempt.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: who must follow whom
slides.body_md: Follow a point of law decided by the Supreme Court down through the courts.
bullets: **Binding** on district courts and High Courts

rows: 1. The Supreme Court decides a point of law
Its decision declares the law for all courts
2. A district court in imagined Varunadesh meets the same point
It must follow the Supreme Court
3. A High Court meets the same point
It must follow the Supreme Court too
Courts then apply the changed law

visual.alt: Worked example table of binding decisions: the Supreme Court decides a point of law; a district court and a High Court meeting the same point must follow it; if Parliament changes the law, courts apply the changed law
visual.caption: Article 141: binding on all courts.

slides.narration: Imagine the Supreme Court decides a point of law. A district court in Varunadesh meets the same point later. It must follow the Supreme Court. A High Court meeting the same point must follow it too. If Parliament changes the law, then the courts apply the changed law. This is the force of Article one hundred and forty one.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Rule of law, disputes, rights, guarding the Constitution
Freedom from interference; not freedom from accountability
President; Chief Justice and collegium decisive since 1993; the 2014 Act struck down in 2015
Retire at 65 and 62; removal by Parliament; Consolidated Fund
Supreme Court, High Courts, district and subordinate courts; Articles 141 and 129

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: need, independence, appointment, tenure and finance, and structure of the judiciary

slides.narration: To sum up. The judiciary upholds the rule of law, settles disputes, protects rights and guards the Constitution. Independence means freedom from interference, not from accountability. Judges are appointed by the President, with the Chief Justice and a collegium decisive since nineteen ninety three. Tenure, finance and protection from debate secure independence. The courts form one hierarchy with the Supreme Court at the top.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Say **freedom from interference**, not freedom from accountability
Use **some argue, others argue** for the appointment debate

rows: Independence means judges are not accountable
Freedom from interference by the legislature and executive; accountability remains
A Chief Minister can remove a High Court judge
Only Parliament, by a special majority, on proved grounds
Judges are appointed by the Chief Justice alone
The President appoints; the Chief Justice and a collegium play the decisive role in recommending

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes in Part 1 and what to write instead

slides.narration: A few tips. When you define independence, say freedom from interference, and not freedom from accountability. When you write about removal, give both the grounds and the special majority. Date your facts, such as nineteen ninety three and twenty fifteen. And for the appointment debate, use the words some argue and others argue.

slides.heading: Judiciary: Jurisdiction and Review
slides.body_md: Part 2: the **jurisdiction** of the Supreme Court, **judicial review**, and **judicial activism**.

Writs
Judicial review
Activism and public interest litigation
Balance with Parliament

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: four jurisdictions, writs, judicial review, activism and public interest litigation, and balance with Parliament
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Which court hears which case, and what can a court do about a law that goes against the Constitution? In this part we study the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, the power of judicial review, the rise of public interest litigation, and the relations between the judiciary and Parliament.

slides.heading: What is jurisdiction?

rows: The authority of a court to hear and decide certain kinds of cases
The court hears the dispute first
The court hears appeals against decisions of lower courts
An order of the court issued to enforce a right
An opinion given without deciding a dispute

visual.alt: Table of terms: jurisdiction is the authority of a court to hear and decide certain cases; original means hearing a dispute first; appellate means hearing appeals; a writ is an order to enforce a right; advisory means giving an opinion without deciding a dispute

slides.narration: Jurisdiction is the authority of a court to hear and decide certain kinds of cases. A court has original jurisdiction when it hears a dispute first, and appellate jurisdiction when it hears appeals against decisions of lower courts. A writ is an order issued to enforce a right. Advisory jurisdiction means giving an opinion without deciding a dispute.

sections.heading: 1. Why an independent judiciary, and what independence means
sections.body_md:
A democracy needs a judiciary for four reasons: it upholds the **rule of law**, **settles disputes**, **protects rights** and **guards the Constitution**.

**Independence of the judiciary** means freedom from interference by the legislature and the executive when judges decide cases. It does **not** mean freedom from accountability: judges are bound by the Constitution, give reasoned judgments in open court, and can be removed for proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

key_terms.definition_md: The organ of government that interprets and applies the law and settles disputes.
The principle that the same law applies to everyone, including the government.
Freedom of the courts from interference by the legislature and the executive in deciding cases.

Decides disputes between citizens, between citizens and the government, and between governments
Enforces Fundamental Rights and other rights against wrongful acts
Examines laws and actions against the Constitution

sections.heading: 2. Appointment of judges and the debate
sections.body_md:
Judges are **appointed by the President**. Since the **Second Judges case (1993)**, the Supreme Court's view is that the **Chief Justice of India and a collegium of senior judges** play the decisive role in recommending names. The **National Judicial Appointments Commission Act (2014)** was **struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015**. This is the position as of 2024.

**Some argue** that the collegium keeps appointments free from pressure by the executive; **others argue** that a wider, accountable body should also take part and that the process should be more open.

key_terms.definition_md: The Chief Justice of India and a group of senior judges who recommend names for appointment as judges.

sections.heading: 3. Tenure, money and other protections
sections.body_md:
- **Security of tenure:** Supreme Court judges retire at **65** and High Court judges at **62**. Removal is only by **Parliament**, on **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**, by a **special majority** in both Houses: a majority of the total membership of each House and at least two thirds of the members present and voting. It is a very difficult process.
- **Financial independence:** salaries and allowances are **charged on the Consolidated Fund of India** and are **not voted on**.
- **Protection from debate:** the conduct of judges **cannot be discussed in the legislature** except during removal proceedings.
- **Contempt:** the courts can **punish for contempt**.

For removal of a judge, a majority of the total membership of each House and at least two thirds of the members present and voting.
The main fund of the Union government; expenses charged on it, such as judges' salaries, are not voted on.

sections.heading: 4. Structure of the judiciary
sections.body_md:
The judiciary is **integrated**: one hierarchy with the **Supreme Court** at the top (the Chief Justice of India and 33 other judges, **34 in all, as of 2024**), **High Courts** in the states, and **district and subordinate courts** below.

- **Article 141:** the law declared by the Supreme Court is **binding on all courts**.
- **Article 129:** the Supreme Court is a **court of record**: its proceedings and decisions are preserved as records and it can punish for its own contempt.

sections.heading: 5. Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
sections.body_md:
**Jurisdiction** is the authority of a court to hear and decide certain cases.

- **Original (Article 131):** disputes between the Union and states, or between states.
- **Writ (Article 32):** enforcement of Fundamental Rights. High Courts have a **wider writ power under Article 226**, covering Fundamental Rights and other legal rights.
- **Appellate:** civil, criminal and constitutional appeals, plus **special leave to appeal (Article 136)**.
- **Advisory (Article 143):** the President can seek the Court's opinion on a question of law or fact of public importance; the opinion is **not binding**.

An order of a court issued to enforce a right.

sections.heading: 7. Judicial activism, PIL and the judiciary and Parliament
sections.body_md:
**Judicial activism** is an active role of the courts in protecting rights and addressing public problems. **Public interest litigation (PIL)** began in the late **1970s and 1980s**: courts relaxed **locus standi**, so any person or group can approach the court on behalf of those who cannot, and **letters and news reports** have been treated as petitions. Examples include prisoners' rights and bonded labour; the **Hussainara Khatoon case (1979)** concerned undertrial prisoners.

**Effects:** wider access to justice and attention to the rights of the poor. **Criticisms some raise:** overburdened courts and **judicial overreach**, which blurs the line between the organs.

**Judiciary and Parliament:** conflicts arose over property rights and Parliament's power to amend; the **Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)** held that Parliament cannot change the basic structure (Chapter 9). The **separation of powers** gives each organ its own role and a system of mutual checks.

A case brought in the public interest by a person or group on behalf of those who cannot approach the court themselves.
The right to bring a case before a court; relaxed by PIL so that others can petition for those who cannot.
The concern, raised by some, that courts enter the field of the legislature or the executive.
The division of government into organs with separate roles that also check one another.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a main reason why a country needs a judiciary that works independently of the other organs of government?

options.text_md: So that the judiciary can make the laws that it then applies
So that disputes are settled and the law is applied impartially, even when the government is one of the parties
So that the courts can choose the ministers of the government
So that the judiciary can raise taxes to meet its own costs

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** So that disputes are settled and the law is applied impartially, even when the government is one of the parties. An independent judiciary applies the law impartially, settles disputes and protects rights, including against the government itself. Making laws belongs to the legislature, choosing ministers to the executive process, and raising taxes to the legislature, so the other options give the judiciary tasks that are not its own.

questions.stem_md: In political theory, the independence of the judiciary means that

options.text_md: judges are not answerable to the law or the Constitution
the judiciary may make laws and run the administration
judges may refuse to hear any case brought by the government
judges decide cases free from interference by the legislature and the executive

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** judges decide cases free from interference by the legislature and the executive. Independence means freedom from interference by the other two organs while deciding cases. It does not place judges above the law, it does not give them the work of the legislature or the executive, and it does not let them refuse cases because the government is a party.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined state of Varunadesh, a minister telephones a High Court judge and urges her to decide a land case in favour of the state government. The judge ignores the call and decides the case on the evidence. Her conduct shows

options.text_md: independence of the judiciary from the executive in practice
judicial review of a law passed by the legislature
the advisory jurisdiction of the High Court
the collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** independence of the judiciary from the executive in practice. A judge who decides on the evidence and resists an approach from a minister is acting independently of the executive. No law is being examined, so it is not judicial review; no opinion is sought by the President, so it is not advisory jurisdiction; and collective responsibility concerns ministers answering to the legislature.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, the practice since the Second Judges case (1993) is that names for appointment as judges of the Supreme Court are recommended mainly by

options.text_md: the Prime Minister acting alone
the Lok Sabha, by a vote of its members
the Chief Justice of India together with a collegium of senior judges
the Election Commission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the Chief Justice of India together with a collegium of senior judges. The Supreme Court's view since 1993 is that the Chief Justice of India and a collegium of senior judges play the decisive role in recommending names; the President makes the formal appointment. The Prime Minister acting alone, a vote in the Lok Sabha and the Election Commission have no such role.

questions.stem_md: The National Judicial Appointments Commission Act (2014), which provided for a commission to take part in appointing judges, was struck down by the Supreme Court in
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 2015. The Court struck down the Act in 2015. The year 1993 is that of the Second Judges case, and 2004 and 2019 are not linked to the Act.

questions.stem_md: A judge of the Supreme Court and a judge of a High Court retire at the ages of, respectively,

options.text_md: 65 years and 62 years
62 years and 65 years
60 years and 58 years
70 years and 65 years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 65 years and 62 years. The Supreme Court age is 65 and the High Court age is 62. The second option reverses the two, and the others give ages that the Constitution does not fix for these courts.

questions.stem_md: The Chief Minister of the imagined state of Varunadesh announces that a High Court judge will be dismissed because three of the judge's rulings went against the state government. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The announcement is valid, since the Chief Minister heads the executive of the state
The announcement is valid if the Governor signs the order
The announcement is valid if the state Bar Council agrees
The announcement has no basis: a High Court judge can be removed only by Parliament, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by a special majority in both Houses

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The announcement has no basis: a High Court judge can be removed only by Parliament, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by a special majority in both Houses. Judges can be removed only through Parliament, on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by a special majority in both Houses; unpopular rulings are not a ground. Neither the Chief Minister, the Governor nor a Bar Council has the power to dismiss a High Court judge.

questions.stem_md: During a budget debate in an imagined session, a member suggests that Parliament put the salaries of Supreme Court judges to a vote every year, to show displeasure at some rulings. Which feature of judicial independence makes such a vote unnecessary and improper?

options.text_md: The judges pay their own salaries out of fees collected from litigants
Their salaries and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and are not voted on
The salaries are fixed every year by the Chief Minister of a state
The judges are paid by the political party that recommended them

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Their salaries and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and are not voted on. Charging salaries and allowances on the Consolidated Fund means they are not put to a vote, which protects the judges from financial pressure. Judges do not live on litigants' fees, are not paid by a state Chief Minister, and are not paid by any party.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined debate in Parliament, a member begins to criticise the personal conduct of a judge of the Supreme Court, although no proposal to remove the judge is before the House. The Presiding Officer stops the member because

options.text_md: the conduct of judges cannot be discussed in the legislature except during removal proceedings
judges may be discussed only in the State Legislative Assemblies
Parliament cannot discuss any matter concerning the judiciary at all
a judge can be discussed only if the judge is present in the gallery

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the conduct of judges cannot be discussed in the legislature except during removal proceedings. The conduct of judges cannot be discussed in the legislature except when a proposal for removal is under consideration, and this protects judges from pressure. Parliament can still discuss laws and policies concerning the judiciary, and the other options invent rules.

questions.stem_md: During a hearing in a district court of the imagined state of Varunadesh, a spectator shouts abuse at the judge and tries to stop the proceedings. Which power allows the court to punish the spectator?

options.text_md: The power of judicial review of laws passed by the legislature
The power to punish for contempt of court, which protects the authority and dignity of the courts
The advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 143
The power to remove ministers from office

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The power to punish for contempt of court, which protects the authority and dignity of the courts. Punishing contempt protects the authority and dignity of the courts and the administration of justice, so the court can act against a person who obstructs a hearing. Judicial review concerns laws and actions, advisory jurisdiction concerns an opinion sought by the President, and courts do not remove ministers.

questions.stem_md: A visitor to the imagined town of Sarwal learns that a case which began in the Sarwal district court was finally decided by the Supreme Court, whose ruling then bound courts in every state. The visitor asks why India does not keep separate court systems for each state. The best answer is that

options.text_md: each state keeps a separate system and the Supreme Court only advises it
the legislature of each state hears the final appeals
India has an integrated judiciary, one hierarchy with the Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in the states and district and subordinate courts below
the Council of Ministers decides which court will hear a case

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** India has an integrated judiciary, one hierarchy with the Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in the states and district and subordinate courts below. An integrated judiciary is one unified hierarchy, so appeals travel upward from district courts through the High Court to the Supreme Court. Separate state systems, final appeals before a legislature, and a Council of Ministers choosing courts would all go against this structure and against independence.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, the strength of the Supreme Court of India is

options.text_md: the Chief Justice of India and 24 other judges, 25 in all
the Chief Justice of India and 9 other judges, 10 in all
the Chief Justice of India and 49 other judges, 50 in all
the Chief Justice of India and 33 other judges, 34 in all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the Chief Justice of India and 33 other judges, 34 in all. As of 2024 the strength is 34 in all, including the Chief Justice of India, and Parliament can change the number by law. The other figures are not the present strength.

questions.stem_md: The Supreme Court decides a point of law in a case from the imagined state of Tilmora. Later, a district court in Varunadesh faces the same point of law. According to Article 141, the district court

options.text_md: may ignore it if the government of Varunadesh prefers another view
must refer the matter to the Governor of Varunadesh
must wait for Parliament to pass a new law before deciding
is bound to follow the Supreme Court's decision on that point of law

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** is bound to follow the Supreme Court's decision on that point of law. Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India. A state government cannot override it, the Governor has no role in the matter, and the court need not wait for Parliament.

questions.stem_md: When the Supreme Court is described as a court of record (Article 129), it means that

options.text_md: it keeps the records of all births and deaths in the country
it records the statements of ministers made in Parliament
its proceedings and decisions are preserved as a record that other courts accept, and it can punish for its own contempt
it destroys the records of the lower courts after ten years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** its proceedings and decisions are preserved as a record that other courts accept, and it can punish for its own contempt. A court of record preserves its proceedings and decisions as authoritative records that cannot be questioned in lower courts, and it has the power to punish for contempt of itself. The other options describe unrelated tasks.

questions.stem_md: Which statement presents the debate on the appointment of judges in a balanced way?

options.text_md: The collegium is plainly right and those who question it are plainly wrong
Some argue that the collegium keeps appointments free from pressure by the executive; others argue that a wider and more accountable body should also take part
The executive alone should appoint judges, so the debate is closed
Every argument on one side is false and no argument on the other is

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Some argue that the collegium keeps appointments free from pressure by the executive; others argue that a wider and more accountable body should also take part. A balanced statement sets out the reasons on each side with the words some argue and others argue. The other options take one side or declare the question closed, which is not a balanced presentation of a debated issue.

questions.stem_md: The imagined states of Karnavar and Tilmora disagree over money: Karnavar says that Tilmora owes it a large sum under an old financial arrangement, and Tilmora denies it. Which court can hear the dispute directly, under its original jurisdiction?

options.text_md: The Supreme Court, under Article 131
The High Court of Karnavar, under Article 226
A district court in Tilmora
The Election Commission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Supreme Court, under Article 131. Article 131 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in disputes between the Union and states or between states. A High Court under Article 226 issues writs, a district court of one party would not be neutral, and the Election Commission conducts elections.

questions.stem_md: The Supreme Court's power to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights comes from

options.text_md: Article 131
Article 32
Article 143
Article 356

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Article 32. Article 32 lets a person approach the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Article 131 is original jurisdiction, Article 143 is advisory, and Article 356 concerns the failure of constitutional machinery in a state.

questions.stem_md: A government order in the imagined state of Varunadesh forbids a group of weavers from holding a peaceful meeting. The weavers believe that their Fundamental Right to assemble peacefully has been violated. Where can they go directly?

options.text_md: Only the Supreme Court, and never the High Court
Only a district court, which alone can issue writs
Only the Council of Ministers of the state
Either the Supreme Court under Article 32 or the High Court of the state under Article 226

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Either the Supreme Court under Article 32 or the High Court of the state under Article 226. A person whose Fundamental Right is violated can approach the Supreme Court under Article 32 or a High Court under Article 226. A High Court is not barred, district courts do not issue such writs, and the Council of Ministers is the authority whose order is being challenged.

questions.stem_md: A weavers' cooperative in the imagined state of Tilmora complains that an order of a state department has taken away a legal right that is given by an ordinary state law and is not a Fundamental Right. Where can it file a writ petition?

options.text_md: In the High Court of Tilmora under Article 226, because a High Court can issue writs for legal rights other than Fundamental Rights
Only in the Supreme Court under Article 32, because it covers every legal right
Only in the Supreme Court under Article 131, because the state is a party
Only before the President, who gives a binding opinion under Article 143

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** In the High Court of Tilmora under Article 226, because a High Court can issue writs for legal rights other than Fundamental Rights. Article 226 lets a High Court issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for other legal purposes, so the cooperative can go there. Article 32 is limited to Fundamental Rights, Article 131 covers disputes between governments, and a reference by the President under Article 143 gives an advisory opinion that is not binding and is not a remedy for a litigant.

questions.stem_md: Mehrunissa loses an appeal in the High Court of an imagined state, and no certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court is given. She still wants the Supreme Court to look at the case. Which route can she try?

options.text_md: A request to the President for an advisory opinion under Article 143
A fresh suit under Article 131, as the Union against a state
A petition for special leave to appeal under Article 136, which the Court may grant at its discretion
A writ under Article 32, which the Court must grant as of right

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A petition for special leave to appeal under Article 136, which the Court may grant at its discretion. Article 136 allows the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal, at its discretion. An advisory opinion is sought by the President and not by a litigant, Article 131 covers disputes between governments, and a writ under Article 32 is for Fundamental Rights and is not a matter of right.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined situation, the President refers a question of law of public importance to the Supreme Court under Article 143, and the Court gives its opinion. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The opinion is a judgment that the government must carry out
The opinion is a law as if passed by Parliament
The opinion is advisory and is not binding on the President
The opinion amends the Constitution automatically

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The opinion is advisory and is not binding on the President. Under Article 143 the Court gives an advisory opinion, which is not binding. It is not a judgment between parties, it is not a law passed by Parliament, and it cannot amend the Constitution.

questions.stem_md: Judicial review is the power of the courts to

options.text_md: examine whether a law or an executive action is consistent with the Constitution and declare it invalid if it is not
review the performance of every judge each year
decide who will be the next Prime Minister
revise the voters' lists prepared by the Election Commission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** examine whether a law or an executive action is consistent with the Constitution and declare it invalid if it is not. Judicial review is the power to test laws and executive actions against the Constitution and declare them invalid if inconsistent. The other options describe unrelated tasks of other bodies.

questions.stem_md: The Legislative Assembly of the imagined state of Varunadesh passes a law that bans all peaceful public meetings in the state for a full year. A petitioner challenges it, and the High Court declares it invalid because it conflicts with Fundamental Rights. This is an example of

options.text_md: the advisory jurisdiction of the High Court
the pocket veto
collective responsibility
judicial review

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** judicial review. A court examining a law against the Constitution and declaring it invalid is exercising judicial review. Advisory jurisdiction involves an opinion sought by the President, the pocket veto is a delay in assent to a bill, and collective responsibility is about ministers and the legislature.

questions.stem_md: Which Article declares laws that are inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights void to that extent, and so supports the courts' power of judicial review?

options.text_md: Article 21
Article 13
Article 74
Article 368

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Article 13. Article 13 provides that laws inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights are void to that extent. Article 21 protects life and personal liberty, Article 74 deals with the Council of Ministers, and Article 368 deals with amendment of the Constitution.

questions.stem_md: An imagined newspaper reports that workers in a stone quarry in Varunadesh are kept in debt bondage. A teacher who is not related to any of them writes a letter to the High Court describing the matter, and the Court treats the letter as a petition. This is an example of

options.text_md: public interest litigation
an advisory opinion
original jurisdiction in a dispute between states
the impeachment of a judge

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** public interest litigation. A person who is not directly affected approaches the court on behalf of those who cannot, and the court treats a letter as a petition: this is public interest litigation. The other options involve the President, two states, or Parliament removing a judge.

questions.stem_md: Before public interest litigation, a court in the imagined town of Sarwal would have rejected a petition by a social worker, Rekha, on behalf of homeless sweepers, saying that her own rights were not affected. Which rule would it have applied, and which public interest litigation later relaxed?

options.text_md: Judicial review, which limited petitions to laws made by Parliament
Locus standi, which limited the right to approach the court to the person whose own rights were affected
Original jurisdiction, which limited petitions to disputes between states
Special leave, which limited petitions to appeals from a High Court

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Locus standi, which limited the right to approach the court to the person whose own rights were affected. Locus standi is the right to bring a case, and the older rule limited it to the person whose rights were affected; public interest litigation relaxed it so that Rekha could petition for others. The other options are different ideas about review, original jurisdiction and appeals.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following would ordinarily NOT be treated as public interest litigation?

options.text_md: A group of citizens petitions on behalf of prisoners who have waited for trial for years
A letter to a High Court describes unsafe working conditions of poor labourers
Bholaram sues his neighbour in the imagined town of Sarwal over the boundary of their two private plots
A lawyer petitions for the rights of children who cannot approach the court themselves

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Bholaram sues his neighbour in the imagined town of Sarwal over the boundary of their two private plots. A private dispute between two neighbours about their own land is ordinary litigation and has no public interest element. The other three raise the rights of groups that are poor or unable to approach the court themselves, which is the field of public interest litigation.

questions.stem_md: On a letter about unsafe school buildings, the High Court of the imagined state of Karnavar orders the state to inspect every school and report back within two months. Supporters call this judicial activism. What does the term describe?

options.text_md: The habit of judges of avoiding the decision of any case
The participation of judges in election campaigns
The power of the legislature to appoint judges
An active role of the courts in protecting rights and addressing public problems, sometimes going beyond deciding a dispute between two parties

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** An active role of the courts in protecting rights and addressing public problems, sometimes going beyond deciding a dispute between two parties. Judicial activism is an active role of the courts in protecting rights and tackling public problems, with directions that may go beyond settling a dispute between two parties, as in the order to inspect schools. Avoiding cases, campaigning and legislative appointment are not what the term means.

questions.stem_md: Some critics describe certain instances of judicial activism as judicial overreach. Which statement best expresses the concern behind the term?

options.text_md: Courts hear too few cases from the poor
Courts are not allowed to give any direction to the government
Judges are chosen by the voters in each district
Courts may enter the field of the legislature or the executive, so that the line between the organs is blurred

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Courts may enter the field of the legislature or the executive, so that the line between the organs is blurred. The concern is that the courts may take up tasks of law-making or administration that belong to the other organs. Others reply that courts act to protect rights where other organs have not. The remaining options are not what critics say.

questions.stem_md: The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) is associated with the principle that

options.text_md: Parliament can amend every part of the Constitution without any limit
the President can veto any amendment
Parliament cannot change the basic structure of the Constitution
the Supreme Court cannot examine any amendment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Parliament cannot change the basic structure of the Constitution. The case held that Parliament's power to amend does not extend to changing the basic structure. The other options claim unlimited power, a presidential veto, or no judicial examination, none of which the case held.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A judge of the Supreme Court can be removed only by Parliament, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

**Reason (R):** Security of tenure protects judges from pressure by the executive and the legislature when they decide cases.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: removal is made difficult, through a special majority in both Houses, precisely so that judges can decide without fear of losing office.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The salaries and allowances of Supreme Court judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and are not voted on.

**Reason (R):** Judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by the President.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: the salaries are not voted on because the Constitution charges them on the Consolidated Fund, which protects financial independence, and not because of who makes the appointment.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Supreme Court can declare a law invalid if it violates the Fundamental Rights.

**Reason (R):** The laws made by Parliament are final, and no court can examine them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: this is judicial review, supported by Articles 13 and 32. R is false: courts can test laws against the Constitution, which is the very power described in A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Public interest litigation has widened access to justice for people who are poor or weak.

**Reason (R):** Courts relaxed the rule of locus standi so that any person or group can approach the court on behalf of those who cannot.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: once a concerned person could petition on behalf of others, those who could not afford or reach a court gained access to justice.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The government must always act on the opinion that the Supreme Court gives when the President seeks its advice under Article 143.

**Reason (R):** The President may seek the opinion of the Supreme Court on a question of law or fact of public importance, and the opinion is not binding.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false because an advisory opinion is not binding. R is true, and it is exactly why the government is not bound to act on it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Indian judiciary is an integrated judiciary.

**Reason (R):** The Supreme Court is a court of record.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: the judiciary is integrated because one hierarchy runs from the district courts through the High Courts to the Supreme Court; being a court of record is a separate feature of the Supreme Court.

questions.stem_md: Independence of the judiciary means that judges are free from every kind of accountability.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Independence means freedom from interference by the legislature and the executive in deciding cases. Judges remain accountable: they give reasoned judgments, are bound by the Constitution, and can be removed for proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

questions.stem_md: A High Court can issue writs not only for Fundamental Rights but also for other legal rights.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Article 226 gives High Courts a wider writ power than the Supreme Court has under Article 32, which is limited to Fundamental Rights.

questions.stem_md: After the rise of public interest litigation, only the person whose own right was violated can approach the court.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Public interest litigation relaxed locus standi so that any person or group can approach the court on behalf of those who cannot.

questions.stem_md: A judge of the Supreme Court retires at the age of ___ years.
questions.solution_md: Judges of the highest court leave office at 65, three years later than High Court judges, who go at 62.

questions.stem_md: A person whose Fundamental Right is violated can approach the Supreme Court directly under Article ___.
questions.solution_md: Article 32 provides for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights by the Supreme Court; High Courts have a similar and wider power under Article 226.

questions.stem_md: Under Article ___, the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India.
questions.solution_md: Article 141 makes the decisions of the Supreme Court binding on all courts.

questions.stem_md: Match each jurisdiction of the Supreme Court with its description.

options.text_md: Original
Writ
Appellate
Advisory

match_right.text_md: Enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article 32
Opinion sought by the President, which is not binding
Disputes between the Union and states, or between states
Civil, criminal and constitutional appeals, and special leave

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Each jurisdiction has its own kind of case: original (Article 131), writ (Article 32), appellate (including Article 136) and advisory (Article 143).

questions.stem_md: Match each safeguard of judicial independence with the feature that provides it.

options.text_md: Security of tenure
Financial independence
Protection from debate
Authority of the courts

match_right.text_md: Removal only by Parliament on proved misbehaviour or incapacity
Conduct of judges not discussed in the legislature except during removal
Salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund of India

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Tenure, finance, protection from debate and the power to punish contempt each secure a different aspect of independence.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these courts from the lowest to the highest in the integrated judiciary.

options.text_md: Supreme Court of India
District court
High Court of the state
Subordinate court

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). Subordinate courts come below the district court, which is below the High Court of the state, and the Supreme Court is at the top.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events in the order in which they would happen in an imagined public interest litigation in Varunadesh.

options.text_md: After a hearing, the Court gives directions to improve the conditions
The Court treats the letter as a petition and issues notice to the state government
A concerned citizen writes to the High Court about it
A newspaper reports poor conditions in a home for the aged

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). The report comes first, then the letter, then the court taking it up as a petition, and finally the directions after the hearing.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the independence of the judiciary? Does it mean that judges are not accountable to anyone?
questions.solution_md: The meaning of independence and the point that accountability remains.

answer.model_answer_md: **Independence** means that judges decide cases **free from interference by the legislature and the executive**. It does **not** mean that judges are above accountability: they are bound by the Constitution, give reasoned judgments and can be removed for **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.

marking_scheme.step: Freedom from interference by the legislature and the executive
Not freedom from accountability; removal possible on proved grounds

questions.stem_md: State any two reasons why a democracy needs an independent judiciary.
questions.solution_md: Two of the four roles: rule of law, settling disputes, protecting rights, guarding the Constitution.

answer.model_answer_md: First, it upholds the **rule of law**, so that the law applies equally to everyone, including the government. Second, it **protects rights** and settles disputes impartially, and it **guards the Constitution** by examining laws and actions that may go against it.

questions.stem_md: A group of members of an imagined legislature demands that a judge be dismissed because they dislike three of her rulings. Why can the demand not succeed? State who can remove a judge and on what grounds.
questions.solution_md: The body that removes, the grounds, and the protection that results, applied to the demand.

answer.model_answer_md: Only **Parliament** can remove a judge, on the grounds of **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**, by a **special majority in both Houses**. Unwelcome rulings are not such grounds, and because removal is very difficult, judges can decide cases without fear of losing office.

marking_scheme.step: Only Parliament, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by a special majority
Unwelcome rulings are no ground, so judges are free from pressure

questions.stem_md: Members in an imagined session of Parliament propose to cut the pay of Supreme Court judges after a ruling that they dislike. Explain how the financial arrangements for judges stop such pressure.
questions.solution_md: The Consolidated Fund and the absence of a vote, applied to the proposal.

answer.model_answer_md: The **salaries and allowances** of Supreme Court judges are **charged on the Consolidated Fund of India**, which means that they are **not voted on** by the legislature. So the proposal cannot be used as a means of pressure, and judges can decide cases without fear of a cut in their pay.

marking_scheme.step: Salaries and allowances charged on the Consolidated Fund and not voted on
So a cut cannot be used as pressure after a ruling

questions.stem_md: What is meant by saying that the Supreme Court is a court of record?
questions.solution_md: Records preserved and accepted, and the contempt power.

answer.model_answer_md: Under **Article 129**, the Supreme Court is a **court of record**. Its **proceedings and decisions are preserved** as authoritative records, which lower courts accept as precedents, and it has the **power to punish for contempt** of itself.

marking_scheme.step: Proceedings and decisions preserved as authoritative records
Power to punish for contempt of itself

questions.stem_md: A High Court in the imagined state of Varunadesh decides a point of law differently from an earlier ruling of the Supreme Court on the same point. Which constitutional provision does this go against, and why?
questions.solution_md: Article 141 applied to the case.

answer.model_answer_md: It goes against **Article 141**, under which the law declared by the **Supreme Court is binding on all courts** in India. In an integrated judiciary the High Court is below the Supreme Court, so it must follow the Court's ruling on that point of law.

marking_scheme.step: Article 141: Supreme Court decisions bind all courts
The High Court is below the Supreme Court in one hierarchy

questions.stem_md: Distinguish the writ power of the Supreme Court under Article 32 from that of a High Court under Article 226 in two points.
questions.solution_md: Scope of the two Articles.

answer.model_answer_md: **Article 32** is itself a Fundamental Right and covers only the **enforcement of Fundamental Rights**. **Article 226** lets a High Court issue writs for Fundamental Rights and also for **other legal rights**, so its writ power is **wider**, though it operates within the High Court's own area.

marking_scheme.step: Article 226: Fundamental Rights and other legal rights, so wider

questions.stem_md: Define judicial review and state where in the Constitution it is rooted.
questions.solution_md: Definition and sources.

answer.model_answer_md: **Judicial review** is the courts' power to test a **law or an executive action against the Constitution** and to declare it **invalid** when it conflicts with it. The words do not appear in the text, but the power flows from **Articles 13, 32 and 226** and others.

marking_scheme.step: Power to examine laws and actions against the Constitution and declare them invalid

questions.stem_md: What is locus standi? How did public interest litigation change it?
questions.solution_md: The meaning of the term and the relaxation.

answer.model_answer_md: **Locus standi** is the right to bring a case before a court, which earlier belonged only to the person whose own right was affected. **Public interest litigation relaxed** it, so that **any person or group** can approach the court on behalf of those who cannot do so themselves.

marking_scheme.step: Locus standi: the right to approach the court, earlier only for the person affected
Relaxed so that others can petition on behalf of those who cannot

questions.stem_md: What is the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court? Is its opinion binding?
questions.solution_md: Article 143, who asks, and the non-binding nature.

answer.model_answer_md: Under **Article 143**, the **President can seek the opinion** of the Supreme Court on a question of law or fact of public importance. The Court gives an **advisory opinion**, which is **not binding** on the President or the government.

marking_scheme.step: The President can seek the Court's opinion under Article 143
The opinion is advisory and not binding

questions.stem_md: Describe any three ways in which the independence of the judiciary is secured in India.
questions.solution_md: Three safeguards, each described.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Security of tenure:** a judge can be removed only by Parliament, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by a special majority.
2. **Financial independence:** the pay and allowances of judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, so the legislature does not vote on them.
3. **Protection from debate and the contempt power:** judges' conduct cannot be discussed in the legislature except in removal proceedings, and courts can punish for contempt.

marking_scheme.step: Another safeguard: protection from debate or contempt power

questions.stem_md: State the position since 1993 on the recommendation of judges for appointment, say what happened to the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act (2014), and give one argument on each side of the debate.
questions.solution_md: The 1993 position, the 2015 decision and the two sides.

answer.model_answer_md: Judges are appointed by the President, but since the **Second Judges case (1993)** the Supreme Court's view is that the **Chief Justice of India and a collegium** play the decisive role in recommending names. The **2014 Act was struck down in 2015**. Some argue that this protects independence; others argue that a wider body should take part for accountability.

marking_scheme.step: Chief Justice of India and a collegium decisive since 1993
NJAC Act (2014) struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015

questions.stem_md: Describe the original, writ and advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
questions.solution_md: Three jurisdictions with their Articles.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Original (Article 131):** disputes between the Union and states, or between states, are heard directly by the Court.
2. **Writ (Article 32):** a person whose Fundamental Right is violated can approach the Court for its enforcement.
3. **Advisory (Article 143):** when the President asks for its opinion on a question of law or fact of public importance, the Court gives one, but it does not bind.

marking_scheme.step: Advisory jurisdiction and its non-binding nature

questions.stem_md: Explain, with an imagined example, how public interest litigation has widened access to justice.
questions.solution_md: Relaxed standing, letters as petitions, and an example.

answer.model_answer_md: Courts **relaxed locus standi**, so any person or group can petition for those who cannot approach the court, and even **letters and news reports** have been treated as petitions. For example, a teacher in imagined Varunadesh could write to the High Court about the plight of **bonded labourers** who cannot themselves go to court.

marking_scheme.step: Letters and news reports treated as petitions

questions.stem_md: State three concerns that some people raise about judicial activism and public interest litigation.
questions.solution_md: Three concerns framed as views.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Some argue that the courts have become **overburdened** with petitions, which can delay other cases.
2. Some argue that this can **blur the line between the organs**, which they call judicial overreach, when courts take up work of the legislature or executive.
3. Some argue that courts lack the means to **supervise the administration** and the working of their own directions.

marking_scheme.step: Blurring of the line between the organs (judicial overreach)
Another concern, such as limits in supervising directions

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of the Indian judiciary and name two features of its integrated character.
questions.solution_md: The three tiers and two features.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Supreme Court** is at the top, **High Courts** work in the states, and **district and subordinate courts** are below them. It is an **integrated judiciary**: one hierarchy, and the **decisions of the Supreme Court bind all courts (Article 141)**; the Supreme Court is also a **court of record (Article 129)**.

marking_scheme.step: Supreme Court, High Courts and district and subordinate courts
One hierarchy: Supreme Court decisions bind all courts

questions.stem_md: Explain, with two examples, how the judiciary and Parliament came into conflict and why the balance between the organs matters.
questions.solution_md: Two sources of conflict, the 1973 case and the idea of balance.

answer.model_answer_md: Conflicts arose over **property rights** and over **Parliament's power to amend the Constitution**. In the **Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)** the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot change the **basic structure**. Under the **separation of powers**, each organ has its own role and checks the others, so the balance protects against the misuse of power.

marking_scheme.step: Conflicts over property rights and amending power
Separation of powers and checks keep the balance

questions.stem_md: Explain why an independent judiciary is needed in a democracy and how its independence is secured in India.
questions.solution_md: The need, the meaning, appointment, tenure and the remaining safeguards.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. An independent judiciary upholds the **rule of law**, settles disputes, **protects rights** and **guards the Constitution**.
2. Independence means freedom from interference by the legislature and executive, not freedom from accountability.
3. Judges are appointed by the **President**, with the **Chief Justice of India and a collegium** playing the decisive role since 1993.
4. **Security of tenure:** retirement at 65 (Supreme Court) and 62 (High Court); removal only by Parliament by a special majority.
5. **Financial independence** (Consolidated Fund), protection from debate, and the **contempt** power.

marking_scheme.step: Need: rule of law, disputes, rights, Constitution
Meaning: freedom from interference, not from accountability
Appointment: President, with the Chief Justice and collegium
Financial independence, protection from debate and contempt

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of the Indian judiciary and explain why it is called integrated.
questions.solution_md: Three tiers, the strength, integration, Articles 141 and 129.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Supreme Court** is at the top, with the **Chief Justice of India and 33 other judges, 34 in all, as of 2024**.
2. **High Courts** work in the states.
3. **District and subordinate courts** work below the High Courts.
4. It is **integrated** because one hierarchy runs through all levels, not separate systems for the Union and the states.
5. The Supreme Court's decisions are **binding on all courts (Article 141)** and it is a **court of record (Article 129)**.

marking_scheme.step: Supreme Court at the top and its strength

questions.stem_md: Explain the original, writ, appellate and advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
questions.solution_md: Each jurisdiction with its Article, plus the High Court writ power.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Original (Article 131):** disputes between the Union and states, or between states, begin in the Supreme Court.
2. **Writ (Article 32):** a person whose Fundamental Right is violated can approach the Court directly; High Courts have a wider power under **Article 226**.
3. **Appellate:** civil, criminal and constitutional appeals.
4. **Special leave (Article 136):** the Court may grant leave to appeal at its discretion.
5. **Advisory (Article 143):** the President can seek its opinion, which is **not binding**.

marking_scheme.step: Advisory jurisdiction and its non-binding nature

questions.stem_md: What is judicial review? Explain its sources, how it works and why it matters for a constitutional democracy.
questions.solution_md: Definition, effect, sources, working and importance.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Judicial review** is the power of the courts to examine whether a **law or an executive action is consistent with the Constitution**.
2. If it is inconsistent, the court can declare it **invalid**.
3. The power is not named as such in the text but flows from **Articles 13, 32, 226** and others; Article 13 makes laws against Fundamental Rights void.
4. Courts usually act when a petitioner challenges a law or an action.
5. It keeps every organ within the Constitution and protects rights.

marking_scheme.step: How it works through a petition
Importance for rights and a limited government

questions.stem_md: Explain what is meant by public interest litigation and discuss its effects and the criticisms that are made of judicial activism.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, origins, effects, criticisms and a balanced conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Public interest litigation** began in the late **1970s and 1980s**, as courts relaxed **locus standi** so that any person or group can approach the court for those who cannot.
2. Even **letters and news reports** have been treated as petitions, for example on prisoners' rights or bonded labour.
3. **Effects:** people who could not reach a court now find **access to justice**, and the **rights of the poor** receive attention.
4. **Criticisms:** some argue that courts are **overburdened**, and that **judicial overreach** blurs the line between the organs.
5. Others reply that courts act where rights would otherwise go unprotected; a balanced view weighs both.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning and origins in the 1970s and 1980s
Letters and reports treated as petitions, with examples
Effects: access to justice and the rights of the poor
Criticisms: overburdened courts and judicial overreach

questions.stem_md: Examine the relations between the judiciary and Parliament, and explain how the separation of powers keeps a balance.
questions.solution_md: Conflicts, the 1973 case, the separation of powers, checks and a reasoned conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Early conflicts arose over **property rights** and over how far **Parliament could amend** the Constitution.
2. In the **Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)**, the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot change the **basic structure** (studied in a later chapter).
3. Under the **separation of powers**, each organ has its own role.
4. Courts check the others through **judicial review**; Parliament makes laws, can amend the Constitution within limits, and can remove judges by a special majority.
5. Some argue the balance has served rights; others argue each organ must avoid entering the field of another.

marking_scheme.step: Conflicts over property rights and amending power
Mutual checks: judicial review and removal of judges

questions.stem_md: Read the briefing note and answer the questions that follow. *(An imagined note written by SOYL for practice; the states, the department and the people are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** A dispute between states begins in the Supreme Court.

**(b)** Article 32 provides for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

**(c) (i)** Article 226 and its wider scope.

**OR (c) (ii)** Neutrality and the Court's position.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Original jurisdiction** (Article 131).

**(b)** **Article 32**.

**(c) (i)** Yes. A High Court can issue writs under **Article 226**. Its power is **wider** than that of the Supreme Court under Article 32, because it covers **Fundamental Rights and other legal rights**.

**OR (c) (ii)** A court of one state could be **seen as partial** to its own state. The Supreme Court, as the **highest court of the Union**, is a **neutral forum** for a dispute between governments, and it can interpret the Constitution authoritatively.

questions.passage_md:

Karnavar says that the neighbouring state of Tilmora owes it a large sum under an agreement on a jointly run power plant. Talks between the two governments have failed, and Karnavar's legal advisers are considering moving the Supreme Court. Separately, Devika, a shopkeeper in Karnavar, found her shop sealed by an order of the district administration issued without any notice. She says that her Fundamental Right to carry on her trade has been violated, and wants to go to court quickly.

marking_scheme.step: Covers Fundamental Rights and other legal rights

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Why is it appropriate that a dispute between two states is heard directly by the Supreme Court and not by a court of one of the states?

answer.model_answer_md: A court of one state could be **seen as partial** to its own state. The Supreme Court, as the **highest court of the Union**, is a **neutral forum** for a dispute between governments, and it can interpret the Constitution authoritatively.

The Supreme Court is the neutral highest court for such disputes
